failing_part: "raises the AUC and corrects the model's tendency to underestimate the rarer class's probability, so the decision threshold can stay at 0.5"
narrowest_regime: none for the stated purpose; oversampling can shift the operating point of a model whose probabilities will be thresholded and not read as risks, but it is not a default and does not add discrimination
reason: The cited paper reports the opposite: random under/oversampling and SMOTE did not raise AUC, and they strongly OVERestimated the minority-class probability (miscalibration), and shifting the threshold gave similar classification results. My simulation (logistic, prevalence 7.6%, oversampling to 50/50) gave AUC 0.774 vs 0.773, mean predicted risk 0.398 vs true 0.076, and 33% of rows flagged at 0.5 (FPR 0.30). Because oversampling moves the predicted probabilities, 0.5 stops being a principled cut-point for anything but a balanced-cost rule on a miscalibrated score.

citations.cite: van den Goorbergh R, van Smeden M, Timmerman D, Van Calster B. The harm of class imbalance corrections for risk prediction models: illustration and simulation using logistic regression. JAMIA 2022;29(9):1525-1534 (abstract: no higher AUC; minority-class probability strongly overestimated; similar results from shifting the threshold)

bite_note: Default of oversampling inside folds would hand the researcher a miscalibrated risk model with no discrimination gain; the natural alternative (fit unadjusted, judge calibration, choose threshold from costs/utility) changes the reported probabilities and decisions.

failing_part: "when its 95% percentile interval spans 0 there is 'no measurable cost on these rows'" (and the regime ">=10 scored rows")
narrowest_regime: With enough scored rows/events for the metrics to be estimable (calibration slope needs a few dozen events per resample at least), the BBC-CV paired difference is a reasonable selection-corrected contrast; read an interval spanning 0 as 'not distinguishable', not as no cost, unless an equivalence margin is set.
reason: Re-making the flexible pick inside each bootstrap resample and scoring on the out-of-bag rows is the BBC-CV device, and it does remove the selection optimism among the flexible set (slightly conservatively, since the pick uses ~63% of rows); pairing with a pre-specified benchmark is sound. But the percentile interval resamples rows of fixed out-of-fold predictions, so it ignores training-set/CV variability and, at 10 scored rows (and a ~37% out-of-bag subset each time) the signed difference and especially |calibration slope - 1| are nearly uninformative, so an interval spanning 0 is absence of evidence and not evidence of no cost (needs an equivalence margin). Rudin 2019 is a position paper on the myth of a necessary trade-off, not a basis for this estimator.

citations.cite: Tsamardinos I, Greasidou E, Tsagris M, Borboudakis G. Bootstrapping the out-of-sample predictions for efficient and accurate cross-validation. Machine Learning 2018;107:1895-1922 (arXiv 1708.07180: bootstrap the whole selection process on out-of-sample predictions; BBC-CV)
Rudin C. Stop explaining black box machine learning models for high stakes decisions and use interpretable models instead. Nat Mach Intell 2019;1:206-215

bite_note: The 'no measurable cost' wording steers a researcher toward choosing the interpretable model on small data where the interval is simply wide; reporting 'cannot distinguish' with the interval would not.

failing_part: "only flips the sign of that column's own coefficient" / "changes no reported number" / "any ... model family"
narrowest_regime: Linear, GLM and penalized-linear models with an intercept and indicator coding: the exposure coefficient, its interval, the fitted values and all other covariates' coefficients are unchanged and the relabeled column's coefficient flips sign, but the intercept (and its SE/interval) also changes; for tree/network learners fitted values are unchanged only up to tie-breaking and seed.
reason: The invariance is right and Frisch-Waugh-Lovell (column space of {1, x} equals that of {1, 1-x}) is the right reason for the exposure coefficient. But with x' = 1 - x the model a + b x = (a + b) + (-b) x', so the intercept moves from a to a + b (my OLS run: 0.974 to 1.526 with a different SE and CI; logit and lasso identical pattern), which is a reported number. The 'any model family' reach is also beyond what the linear algebra gives.

citations.cite: Frisch R, Waugh FV (1933) Econometrica 1:387-401; Lovell MC (1963) JASA 58:993-1010

bite_note: The exposure estimate and its interval, the quantities the researcher acts on, are unchanged, so skipping the post-lock check on them is right; only the intercept (reference-group prediction) shifts.

failing_part: "(age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, income/poverty ratio, occupation, marital status) are pre-exposure common causes ... (after exposure no)" for "any study design, including cross-sectional"
narrowest_regime: Age and sex (and, with caveats, race/ethnicity as a proxy for social exposures, and adult education that was completed before the exposure window) when the exposure is a habitual/lifelong or later measured behaviour; income, occupation and marital status only when measured before the exposure or when reverse causation from health and mediation are implausible.
reason: VanderWeele's guidance is to adjust for pre-exposure causes of exposure or outcome, and to be careful when temporal order is uncertain; in a cross-sectional survey income/poverty ratio, occupation and marital status are measured at the same time as the exposure and the outcome and can be consequences of the exposure (mediators, e.g. diet to health to income) or of the outcome (illness to job loss, income loss, divorce). Pre-filling 'after exposure: no' for the whole list misclassifies those as plain confounders, and race/ethnicity is not itself a cause (it stands for social conditions). A one-tap confirmation makes the wrong default likely to stick.

citations.cite: VanderWeele TJ. Principles of confounder selection. Eur J Epidemiol 2019;34:211-219
VanderWeele TJ, Robinson WR. On the causal interpretation of race in regressions adjusting for confounding and mediating variables. Epidemiology 2014;25:473-484

bite_note: Adjusting for a mediator or a reverse-causal consequence (income, occupation, marital status) shifts the total-effect estimate (over-adjustment bias), which the researcher would avoid if each variable's timing were asked.

failing_part: "200 by default" percentile resamples and the "at least 90%" floor (no methods basis); the caveat about dropped resamples is directionally right
narrowest_regime: Direction of the caveat holds whenever dropped resamples are those with low estimated reliability (large corrected coefficients); the constants 200 and 90% have no derivation.
reason: Dropping resamples where the estimated within-person variance swamps the between-person variance removes the resamples with the largest corrected coefficients (beta_naive / lambda-hat), so the far end of the percentile interval is pulled in: the caveat is correct. But 200 is the size used for a bootstrap standard error, while percentile endpoints are usually run with at least 1000 resamples, and the 90% floor is declared to be 'a stated floor'. In my simulation (two recalls, lambda about 0.3, n 60-80) the intervals shown had about nominal overall coverage (0.95) yet 11% one-sided misses above when almost no resamples were dropped, so the rule neither clearly protects nor clearly fails.

citations.cite: Efron B, Tibshirani RJ. An Introduction to the Bootstrap. Chapman & Hall 1993, ch. 13 (B of about 50-200 for SE, at least 1000 for percentile intervals)
Carroll RJ, Ruppert D, Stefanski LA, Crainiceanu CM. Measurement Error in Nonlinear Models, 2nd ed., 2006 (regression calibration, bootstrap)

bite_note: Only in the low-reliability regime: the floor decides whether the researcher sees an interval at all for the corrected coefficient; at reliability above about 0.4 it never triggers and B=200 vs 1000 moves the endpoints modestly.

failing_part: "rows are dropped only for blanks in the predictors" and "Blanks ... coded as their own 'Missing' level are values, not missing data"
narrowest_regime: Holds as a description of the app's row rule when the outcome and exposure are handled separately; it is not complete-case analysis for the columns coded as a Missing level.
reason: Complete-case analysis drops any row with a blank in any analysis variable including the outcome (and the exposure), so 'only predictors' is not the definition. Coding blanks as a Missing level keeps those rows and is the missing-indicator method, not complete cases: the blanks are still missing data, and for estimation/explanation it is known to leave bias (residual confounding, distorted coefficients) unless the data are MCAR and effects are additive. Leaving unconfirmed roles out of the row filter and waiting for confirmation is a sensible design.

citations.cite: Groenwold RHH et al. Missing covariate data in clinical research: when and when not to use the missing-indicator method for analysis. CMAJ 2012;184:1265-1269
Sperrin M et al. Missing data should be handled differently for prediction than for description or causal explanation. J Clin Epidemiol 2020;125:183-187

bite_note: Which rows are in the fit (n, and which respondents) differs, and for an Estimate goal a confounder coded as a Missing level gives a different, possibly biased, exposure coefficient than true complete cases.

failing_part: "at least 10 rows and ... at least 5 rows of each class" (thresholds with no stated or derivable justification)
narrowest_regime: Direction (do not score tiny subgroups, and show an interval) is sound; a threshold of 10/5 is far below what makes a discrimination or calibration estimate usable, so it is a display floor only.
reason: TRIPOD+AI asks for performance, with intervals, in key subgroups but gives no minimum size, and the claimed basis admits 'thresholds: none stated'. With 5 events and 5 non-events the AUC standard error is about 0.14-0.15 and a calibration slope is not estimable, so the cut-offs are conventions without methods grounding; sample-size work for validation points to at least 100 events and 100 non-events for stable estimates. Tertile grouping of an amount at the 1/3 and 2/3 quantiles is an arbitrary but harmless convention.

citations.cite: Collins GS et al. TRIPOD+AI statement. BMJ 2024;385:e078378
Collins GS, Ogundimu EO, Altman DG. Sample size considerations for the external validation of a multivariable prognostic model. Stat Med 2016;35:214-226
Riley RD et al. Minimum sample size for external validation of a clinical prediction model with a binary outcome. Stat Med 2021;40:4230-4251

bite_note: The interval shown at small n is very wide and carries the uncertainty, so the 10/5 floor only toggles borderline groups; a reader will not act differently on a scored versus unscored group of 8-15 rows.

narrowest_regime: Holds as stated; the non-collapsibility reason applies only to OR/HR (and common outcomes); for collapsible measures the block rests on the first reason and on post-selection inference.
reason: A change in the exposure coefficient on adding a covariate is produced equally by confounders, mediators and colliders, so the rule cannot separate them, and for odds and hazard ratios adding a pure outcome predictor changes the conditional OR/HR with no confounding because these measures are non-collapsible. The block-and-record action is a policy built on those two facts; note that Maldonado and Greenland found a 10% change rule performs acceptably for confounder selection among valid candidates on collapsible scales, so the block is a conservative choice, not a theorem.

citations.cite: Greenland S, Pearl J, Robins JM. Confounding and collapsibility in causal inference. Stat Sci 1999;14:29-46
Maldonado G, Greenland S. Simulation study of confounder-selection strategies. Am J Epidemiol 1993;138:923-936
Hernan MA. The hazards of hazard ratios. Epidemiology 2010;21:13-15

bite_note: Blocks a data-driven covariate drop that would otherwise change the OR/HR for non-causal reasons and invalidate post-selection intervals; the alternative is a pre-specified adjustment set.

narrowest_regime: Holds as stated for k >= 3 cycles. The log-scale pooled value back-transformed is a geometric-mean (typical-cycle) MSE, which for between-cycle heterogeneity is below the arithmetic-mean MSE, so it is not the 'average MSE' unless that caveat is shown; the prediction interval back-transforms validly.
reason: Standard error of an MSE is proportional to the MSE (about MSE*sqrt(2/n) for Gaussian errors), so inverse-variance weights on the identity scale favour cycles with small (and by chance small-estimated) MSE and pull the pooled MSE down. My simulation with equal true MSE and n=100 gave an identity-scale pooled MSE of 0.971 vs 1.000, and with heterogeneity (log-sd 0.6, n=100) 1.07 vs a true mean 1.20; the log scale has an approximately constant variance 2/n, so weights no longer depend on the level. The t(k-2) prediction interval is Higgins et al.'s; the HKSJ interval for the mean uses t(k-1).

citations.cite: Riley RD et al. External validation of clinical prediction models using big datasets from e-health records or IPD meta-analysis. BMJ 2016;353:i3140
Higgins JPT, Thompson SG, Spiegelhalter DJ. A re-evaluation of random-effects meta-analysis. JRSS A 2009;172:137-159 (prediction interval on t_{k-2})

IntHout J, Ioannidis JPA, Borm GF. The Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman method for random effects meta-analysis is straightforward and considerably outperforms the standard DerSimonian-Laird method. BMC Med Res Methodol 2014;14:25

Snell KIE et al. Meta-analysis of prediction model performance across multiple studies: which scale helps ensure between-study normality for the C-statistic and calibration measures? Stat Methods Med Res 2018;27:3505-3522

bite_note: Changes the pooled cross-cycle MSE (by a few to ten percent in my runs) and the prediction interval for a new cycle, which are the numbers reported as the development estimate.

narrowest_regime: Holds as stated; 'recorded at that moment' should be read as 'available by that moment' (earlier-recorded predictors are legitimate).
reason: PROBAST item 2.3 asks whether all predictors are available at the time the model is intended to be used, and a predictor obtainable only later (later labs, a recall not taken in the clinic) inflates apparent performance relative to deployment, or makes the model unusable. Excluding such columns by default is the right protection.

citations.cite: Moons KGM et al. PROBAST: a tool to assess risk of bias and applicability of prediction model studies. Ann Intern Med 2019;170:W1-W33 (item 2.3)

bite_note: Determines which columns enter the model; dropping a later-known predictor lowers apparent performance to what the clinic can achieve.

failing_part: "estimates the surveyed population's performance without bias, because randomly drawn folds are themselves simple random samples of the design"
narrowest_regime: Unweighted random-row CV is unbiased for the population only if the design is equal-probability and un-clustered (or performance does not vary with the weights); it estimates performance on the sample's own composition.
reason: Folds drawn at random from a weighted sample inherit the unequal selection probabilities and clustering, so they are not simple random samples of the population; the unweighted mean loss estimates the sample-average loss and ignores design weights. In my simulation (stratum with 20% of the population but 50% of the sample and 9x the error variance) unweighted 5-fold CV gave MSE 5.02 against a population value of 2.60, and design-weighted CV gave 2.62; clustered designs also leak PSU information across folds. Wieczorek et al. propose design-weighted, cluster-respecting CV for this reason.

citations.cite: Wieczorek J, Guerin C, McMahon T. K-fold cross-validation for complex sample surveys. Stat 2022;11:e454
Karim ME, Hossain MB. arXiv 2607.10634 (naive K-fold CV optimistic on new clusters as ICC rises)

bite_note: Changes the CV design offered for survey data and the reported population performance (biased estimate vs design-weighted, cluster-respecting folds), including model selection by CV.

narrowest_regime: Plain OLS with non-robust, HC or cluster-robust standard errors. Row order would matter for HAC (Newey-West) intervals, for CV fold assignment, or for an iterative/SGD solver, none of which is plain least squares.
reason: X'X = sum x_i x_i' and X'y = sum x_i y_i are sums over rows, so coefficients, the residual variance, the covariance matrix and the (row-aligned) fitted values are invariant to permutation up to floating-point error; shuffling before OLS is therefore a no-op and skipping it is harmless.
bite_note: Shuffling or not gives identical OLS output, so the default changes nothing the researcher sees.
